answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 (text as amended by Ley 18.252 of 1983 and Ley 19.476 of 1996) dealt with asylum and refugees in arts. 34-40. Art. 39 barred expelling a refugee or asylee to a country where they were in danger, but no provision required anyone to be told that asylum might be available before expulsion or refusal of entry. There was no rule to apply, so no practice evidence was looked for.

Same DL 1.094 refugee provisions (version in force 31-05-2002 to 14-04-2010, read). Ley 19.880 (2003) sets general rights in administrative procedure but has no duty to inform about asylum. No change.
Unchanged until Ley 20.430 entered into force on 15-04-2010, after this date. No duty to inform about asylum.

Ley 20.430 (arts. 3-4: non-refoulement, including no rejection at the border; art. 27: officials who learn of an application must pass it on) and Decreto 837/2010 (art. 6: non-refoulement applies once the person says they intend to apply; art. 38: the applicant is informed of the procedure only after the application is formally lodged). None of these requires telling a person, before expulsion or refusal of entry, that asylum may be available.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.what_changed: Added non-refoulement for refugees, asylees and asylum applicants. It does not create a duty to inform anyone about asylum.

events.what_changed: New refugee law: non-refoulement including no rejection at the border; officials must pass on applications they learn of. It has no duty to advise people that asylum is available. It repealed the DL 1.094 provisions on refugees.

events.what_changed: Information on the procedure is given only after the application is formally lodged. Non-refoulement applies from the moment the person states an intention to apply. Neither requires advising anyone before expulsion or refusal of entry.

answers.repealed_search: I read the DL 1.094 refugee and asylum articles in the 1975, 2002-2010 and 2011-2022 versions, Ley 20.430 arts. 3-5, 15 and 26-28, and Decreto 837 arts. 5-7 and 38 as originally published. None of them, at any point between 2000 and 2020, required anyone to be advised that asylum was available before expulsion or refusal of entry. No repealed protection found.
answers.sourcing_note: I read the LeyChile versions of DL 1.094 in force 2002-2010 and 2011-2022, plus its 1975 original. LeyChile shows a single version for 1975-2002, so the text in force in 2000 was rebuilt from the Ley 18.252 and Ley 19.476 annotations in the 2002 version. I read Ley 20.430 only in its current text, and Decreto 837 in its 2011 original.
answers.notes: No change across the period. Since 2010, the obligations of border officials are framed as non-refoulement and transmitting applications, not as advising people. The current text of Ley 20.430 includes the 2024 Ley 21.655 amendments, which are outside the period.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 art. 39 (Ley 19.476, 1996) barred expelling a refugee, asylee or asylum applicant 'hacia el país donde su vida o libertad peligre' (to the country where their life or liberty is in danger). It says nothing about expulsion to a third country that might in turn expel the person.
Art. 39 is unchanged in the version in force 2002-2010 (read). No chain-refoulement ban.
Same art. 39. Ley 20.430 entered into force only on 15-04-2010.

Ley 20.430 art. 4 and Decreto 837 art. 6 bar return 'al país donde su vida o libertad personal peligren' and 'hacia las fronteras de un país donde estuviere en peligro la seguridad'. Ley 20.430 art. 5 gives an expelled refugee 30 days to seek admission elsewhere. Neither bans expulsion to a country that would re-expel the person to danger.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.what_changed: Direct non-refoulement only: no expulsion to the country where life or liberty is in danger. Nothing on chain refoulement.
events.passage: Artículo 39.- Un refugiado o asilado político no podrá ser expulsado hacia el país donde su vida o libertad peligre por causa de su raza, religión, nacionalidad, pertenencia a determinados grupos sociales u opiniones políticas.

events.what_changed: Replaced DL 1.094 art. 39 with broader non-refoulement, extended to torture risk, and an exceptional expulsion regime for refugees. There is no explicit bar on indirect (chain) refoulement.
events.passage: No procederá la expulsión o cualquier medida que tenga por efecto la devolución, incluyendo la prohibición de ingreso en frontera, de un solicitante de la condición de refugiado o refugiado al país donde su vida o libertad personal peligren.

events.what_changed: The regulation repeats the non-refoulement wording and the 30-day period to seek admission in another country. It has no chain-refoulement ban.
events.passage: se le deberá conceder un plazo de treinta días para que gestione su admisión legal en otro país

answers.repealed_search: I read the DL 1.094 1975 text, art. 39 in the 2002-2010 version, Ley 20.430 arts. 4-5 and Decreto 837 arts. 6-7. None bans expulsion to a third country from which the person would be refouled. No repealed or narrowed protection found.
answers.sourcing_note: I read the versions in force for 2005, 2010 and 2015. The 2000 text was rebuilt from the Ley 19.476 annotations in LeyChile's 2002 version, because LeyChile shows one undifferentiated version for 1975-2002.
answers.notes: One could argue that the second paragraph of Ley 20.430 art. 4 ('cualquier forma de devolución hacia las fronteras de un país donde estuviere en peligro la seguridad de la persona') reaches indirect return. It does not expressly ban expulsion to a country likely to re-expel the person, so the coder's No is kept. In any case these provisions cover only refugees and asylum seekers.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 as amended by Ley 18.252 (1983). Art. 84: expulsion 'será dispuesta por decreto supremo fundado' (ordered by reasoned supreme decree), reserving to the person the administrative and judicial remedies; tourists are expelled by resolution of the Intendente. The grounds are set by law in arts. 15, 17, 63-67, 69 and 87. There is no practice evidence for around 2000, so the 2020 rating is carried over with low confidence.
Arts. 84, 89 and 90 unchanged in the 2002-2010 version (read); Ley 19.806 (2002) did not touch them. There is no specific practice evidence for around 2005, so the rating is inferred.
Same provisions. The CMW's 2011 concluding observations asked Chile to ensure that 'the legal framework which regulates expulsion/deportation procedures is adequately implemented', which shows gaps.

Same provisions (2011-2022 version, read; Ley 20.507 did not change arts. 84/89/90). From 2010, Ley 20.430 art. 5 also allows refugees to be expelled only exceptionally. In 2013 the Supreme Court struck down expulsion decrees as unreasoned and disproportionate, which shows both judicial correction and administrative lapses.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: I read DL 1.094 in the 1975, 2002-2010 and 2011-2022 versions. The 2000 text was rebuilt from the Ley 18.252 (1983) annotations, since LeyChile shows one version for 1975-2002. Practice evidence for 2000 and 2005 is missing; the 2013 and 2019 rulings are known only from press reports.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 answer cannot rest on Ley 21.325 arts. 126-136, which took effect on 12-02-2022. On 1 January 2020 it rests on DL 1.094 art. 84 (reasoned supreme decree) and the statutory grounds. That supports Yes, though tourists could be expelled 'sin más trámite' (without further formality) by Intendente resolution.
answers.notes: The answer is Yes on every date, resting on DL 1.094 art. 84 as amended in 1983. The Supreme Court amparo rulings were read only through press reports and are used as practice evidence only. Ley 19.806 (2002) and Ley 20.507 (2011) created new LeyChile versions but did not change arts. 84, 89 or 90.

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 arts. 89-90 (Ley 18.252, 1983) apply to expulsions by supreme decree. The person may lodge a reasoned claim with the Supreme Court within 24 hours, which must rule within 5 days, and 'la interposición del recurso suspenderá la ejecución' (filing suspends enforcement). The order must be notified in writing. There is no administrative hearing and the deadline is very short. There is no practice evidence for around 2000, so the 2020 rating is carried over with low confidence.

Same arts. 89-90 (2002-2010 version, read). From 29-05-2003 Ley 19.880 art. 10 also lets interested parties put forward allegations at any point in an administrative procedure, applying where no special rule governs. There is no specific practice evidence.
Same provisions. The CMW (2011) found the expulsion appeal 'insufficiently accessible, as illustrated by the short time limit'.

Arts. 89-90 unchanged (2011-2022 version). From 2010, Ley 20.430 art. 5 gives refugees the right to present exculpatory evidence and to challenge expulsion administratively and judicially. Practice: amparos (constitutional habeas petitions) against expulsions were granted by the Supreme Court (2013), and the 24-hour limit drew criticism.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: Arts. 89-90 were read in the 2002-2010 and 2011-2022 LeyChile versions. The 2000 text was rebuilt from the Ley 18.252 (1983) annotations, the 1975 original having been read for comparison. Practice evidence for 2000 and 2005 is missing; the court material comes from press reports.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 citation relies on Ley 21.325 arts. 132 and 141 (the 10-day period to answer the charges and judicial review), which only took effect on 12-02-2022. On 1 January 2020 the answer rests on DL 1.094 arts. 89-90. These gave a 24-hour Supreme Court claim with suspensive effect but no prior administrative hearing, and covered only expulsions by supreme decree; tourists expelled by Intendente resolution had to rely on constitutional amparo. Yes is defensible, but the protection was much thinner than the 2022 regime.
answers.notes: No change in the law between 2000 and 2020. Ley 19.880 (2003) and Ley 20.430 art. 5 (2010, refugees) added to the protection but did not change the answer. No ruling was relied on as law.
